# Office of Kaiju Affairs

**An agent-native government site — where the agent layer is generated by the CMS at publish time, not hand-coded page by page.**

Built for [The WebMCP Challenge](https://devpost.com). MIT licensed.

- **Live site:** <https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app>
- **The Arena:** <https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app/arena/> — a side-by-side race between an agent guessing through the UI and an agent using this site's published tools.

---

## The one-sentence version

A CMS publishes a 51-page government site — public service pages plus the
agency's technical docs corpus, the Kaiju Monitoring Platform. At publish time it also emits a
`manifest.json` describing every page, service, eligibility rule and form — and
one script tag. That script turns the manifest into seven WebMCP tools. Nobody
wrote a tool for a page. Publish a thousand more pages and the agent layer
scales with them, for free.

Then the Arena proves it matters: same three citizen tasks, one agent with the
tools, one without.

## What the site publishes about itself

```js
// runtime/src/register.js — Chrome 150+ exposes document.modelContext.
// navigator.modelContext is the pre-March-2026 location and is deprecated.
const handle = document.modelContext.registerTool({
  name: 'check_eligibility',
  description:
    "Evaluate a person's situation against this agency's published eligibility " +
    'rules and return the outcome, any fee waivers granted, the documents they ' +
    'will need, and a citation to the page that states each rule.',
  inputSchema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      serviceId: { type: 'string', description: 'Service to check, e.g. "damage-compensation".' },
      answers: { type: 'object', description: 'Answers keyed by question id.', additionalProperties: true }
    }
  },
  annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, destructiveHint: false, openWorldHint: false },

  async execute({ serviceId, answers }) {
    const manifest = await getManifest();               // published by the CMS
    const ruleset = manifest.rulesetForService(serviceId);
    return result(evaluate(ruleset, answers));          // rules are data, not prose
  }
});

// Tools belong to the document, so they leave with it.
addEventListener('pagehide', () => handle.unregister());
```

Every published page carries exactly one line:

```html
<script type="module" src="/runtime/kaiju-webmcp.js" data-manifest="/manifest.json"></script>
```

## The seven tools

The budget is seven, and every one maps to a question a person actually walks
into an agency office to ask.

| Tool | The citizen question it answers |
|---|---|
| `search_site` | "Where on earth is that written down?" |
| `get_page_summary` | "Just tell me what this page says." |
| `list_services` | "What can I even do here?" |
| `get_service_requirements` | "What do I need to bring?" |
| `check_eligibility` | "Do I qualify, and for what?" |
| `prefill_permit_form` | "Fill this in for me — I'll check it and submit it." |
| `get_office_info` | "Which office, and how do I get out of Zone 4?" |

Three of them are the interesting ones:

- **`check_eligibility` returns citations, not opinions.** Rules ship as data in
  the manifest. Every outcome names the rule that produced it and the page that
  states it, so nobody has to take the agent's word for it. The person's answers
  are evaluated inside the page — this site is static, so there is no server to
  send them to.
- **`prefill_permit_form` has no code path that submits.** It fills the visible
  fields, highlights them, reports exactly what it entered and what it refused
  to enter, and stops. The handover to the human is structural, not a matter of
  the agent behaving itself.
- **`search_site` searches the generated index**, which is why it finds a rule
  buried in the middle of a 1,500-word FAQ that the navigation never mentions.

## The Arena

`/arena/` runs three citizen tasks in two lanes.

| | UI-guessing lane | WebMCP lane |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | An agent with no tools: reads pages, clicks links, scrolls | The judge's own agent, live, using the registered tools |
| When it ran | Recorded once before submission, saved as JSON traces in `baselines/` | Right now, in your tab |

The page replays the recorded runs step by step with a running timer and action
counter, next to the task card you just completed yourself. Each task ships a
persona to copy into your agent and an answer key to check the result against.

The three tasks:

1. **Needle in the haystack** — find the fee-waiver rule for repeat damage
   claims, buried deep in an FAQ.
2. **Eligibility determination** — given a scenario, determine eligibility and
   list the required documents.
3. **Permit prefill** — complete the kaiju-proximity construction permit
   correctly. *You* submit it.

## Repo layout

```
kaiju-affairs/
  runtime/       the WebMCP runtime every page loads (this is the interesting code)
    kaiju-webmcp.js    entry point — reads the manifest, registers the tools
    src/               manifest indexing, search, rule evaluation, form prefill, registration
    test/smoke.mjs     runtime tests, no browser required
    mock/manifest.json a hand-written manifest for local development
  arena/         the race page — scoreboard, replay theatre, answer keys
  baselines/     recorded UI-lane runs (JSON traces) + the trace schema
  site/          the CMS publish target — the static site and its generated manifest.json
  scaffold/      placeholder pages used only until site/ has content
  docs/          the interface contracts between the CMS, the runtime and the Arena
```

## Running it locally

```bash
npm test        # runtime tests + the content-coupling check. No browser, no dependencies.
npm run check   # coupling check alone, against whatever manifest would deploy
```

The coupling check is the guard on the one seam where content and code are
joined. `arena/answer-keys.json` states the correct answer to each race task,
and those answers are only correct while the published content still says what
it said. The check runs the real rule engine and the real search ranking against
the deployed manifest — if a content edit moves a fee, a threshold or a heading
anchor, the build fails and names the task it broke, rather than a judge finding
out on camera.

```bash
npm run build && node serve.mjs   # http://localhost:4173
```

`build.mjs` assembles `dist/`: the published site at the root, plus
`/runtime/`, `/arena/`, `/baselines/` and `/manifest.json`. Until the CMS
publishes into `site/`, it falls back to the placeholder pages in `scaffold/`
and the mock manifest, so the runtime and the Arena can be developed and tested
in isolation. Any build that used the fallback says so, loudly.

There are no dependencies. Node 18+ and a browser.

## Seeing the tools work

Open the site in Chrome 150+ with WebMCP enabled, or in the ChatGPT in-app
browser, and the Arena's status pill turns green with a self-test button.

**If `document.modelContext` comes back undefined in Chrome, the flag hasn't
taken effect yet.** Enabling it in `chrome://flags` is not enough on its own —
you have to press the blue **Relaunch** button that appears at the bottom of
that page. Quitting and reopening Chrome the normal way does not apply it. Once
relaunched:

```js
// getTools() returns a Promise — await it.
(await document.modelContext.getTools()).map(t => t.name)
// → check_eligibility, get_office_info, get_page_summary, get_service_requirements,
//   list_services, prefill_permit_form, search_site
```

### Calling a tool from the DevTools console

Chrome's current implementation is fussier than you might expect, in four ways
that are easy to trip over: `getTools()` returns a **Promise**, so it has to be
awaited before you can filter it; `executeTool` takes the **tool object** it
resolves to (passing the name string throws `not of type RegisteredTool`); the
arguments must be a **JSON string** (passing an object throws
`Failed to parse input arguments`); and results come back inconsistently
marshalled, so type-check before using them.

This snippet handles all four — paste it whole:

```js
const call = async (name, args = {}) => {
  const tool = (await document.modelContext.getTools()).find(t => t.name === name);
  if (!tool) throw new Error(`no such tool: ${name}`);
  const out = await document.modelContext.executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(args));
  return typeof out === 'string' ? JSON.parse(out) : out;   // marshalling varies
};

await call('search_site', { query: 'fee waiver repeat damage claims' });
await call('check_eligibility', {
  serviceId: 'damage-compensation',
  answers: { zone: '4', structuralDamage: true, incidentsLast12Months: 2,
             propertyType: 'commercial', insurancePayoutReceived: false,
             householdIncomeYen: 3600000, daysSinceIncident: 21 }
});
```

The second call is the Arena's task 2 scenario. It returns `eligible` with three
grants — the assessment-fee waiver, the hardship supplement and
business-interruption eligibility — and the five documents she needs, each with
a citation to the page that states the rule.

Without a WebMCP-capable browser, the tools are still there — the runtime always
exposes them on `window.kaijuWebMCP` so you can call one exactly as an agent
would:

```js
await kaijuWebMCP.call('search_site', { query: 'fee waiver repeat damage claims' })
```

## Why WebMCP, specifically

Agents are already using government sites, by reading rendered HTML and guessing
which link is the right one. On a small, well-structured site that mostly works
— our own recorded baselines say so, and we publish them rather than hide them.
What it costs is time and certainty: seconds and kilobytes of parsed HTML per
question, an answer with no citation attached, and no way for the person reading
it to tell a right answer from a confident wrong one.

WebMCP changes what the site guarantees rather than what the agent manages. The
tools return structured answers with a citation to the page that states each
rule, so a claim can be checked instead of trusted. And the handover to the
human is structural: `prefill_permit_form` has no code path that submits, so a
form cannot be filed on someone's behalf by an agent that decides it knows best.

That distinction is the point, and our own traces sharpen it. The UI-guessing
agent did not submit the permit either — it behaved well, four runs out of four.
But nothing made it behave well. Here, nothing has to.
